name: Pop Rocks (跳跳糖)
blurb: Carbonated candy crystals that crackle and jump on your tongue, around since 1976
title: Pop Rocks: How They Pop, When They Came Out, and Today
description: Pop Rocks are carbonated candy crystals that crackle in your mouth. Launched by General Foods in the US in 1976, a 1990s hit in China as tiaotiaotang.
answer: Pop Rocks are small crystals of hard candy that trap pressurised carbon dioxide, so they crackle and jump on your tongue as they dissolve. General Foods patented the process in 1961, test-marketed the candy in Canada in 1974 and launched it in the US in 1976. In China, Korean-made popping candy called tiaotiaotang (跳跳糖, "jumping candy") was a 1990s playground favourite. Pop Rocks are still made today by Spain's Zeta Espacial.

body: Hot candy syrup is cooled under carbon dioxide at about 50 atmospheres, sealing tiny high-pressure bubbles inside. When the pressure is released the slab shatters into small pieces. In your mouth, saliva dissolves the candy, the bubbles burst, and the fragments crackle and skip around. You tear the little packet open and tip it straight onto your tongue.

body: Soon after launch, a story spread that a child actor from a cereal commercial had died after eating Pop Rocks and drinking cola. It was false; the actor was alive and well. MythBusters later tested the idea on a pig's stomach, which did not burst. The rumour still hurt sales and is part of why General Foods dropped the candy in 1980.

Yes. Zeta Espacial of Barcelona owns the brand and makes it, with Pop Rocks Inc. distributing in the United States. Popping candy is also made by other companies and is often used as a crackling topping in chocolate and desserts.

faq.q: Will Pop Rocks and soda make your stomach explode?
faq.a: No. That is a 1970s urban legend; tests, including on MythBusters, showed nothing of the sort.
Carbon dioxide sealed into the candy under pressure, released as it dissolves.
